blocks.text: A tyre gauge reads 220 kPa on a cold morning, yet the air inside the tyre is at an absolute pressure above 320 kPa. A condenser vacuum gauge reads 'minus 85 kPa' yet the steam inside is far from absolute zero pressure. Engineering formulae need absolute values, and instruments usually show something else.

blocks.markdown: The SI unit of pressure is the **pascal**, $1\ \text{Pa}=1\ \text{N/m}^2$; engineering uses kPa and MPa, and the bar ($10^5$ Pa). Standard atmospheric pressure is about $101.3$ kPa. Pressure instruments such as tyre gauges measure pressure **relative to the surrounding atmosphere**, which is called **gauge pressure**; the true pressure measured from a perfect vacuum is **absolute pressure**.

blocks.caption: Use the first form when the pressure is above atmospheric and the second when a vacuum gauge reads below atmospheric

blocks.title: Gauge to absolute
blocks.prompt: A tyre gauge reads 220 kPa when atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa. A condenser vacuum gauge reads 20 kPa of vacuum at the same atmospheric pressure. Find the absolute pressure in each.

steps.text: Condenser: pressure below atmospheric by 20 kPa.

blocks.answer: The tyre is at 321.3 kPa absolute and the condenser at 81.3 kPa absolute.

blocks.markdown: **Temperature** also needs an absolute scale. The kelvin (K) is the SI unit and starts at absolute zero, while the Celsius scale is offset. For gas laws and efficiency formulae always use kelvin.

blocks.caption: A temperature difference has the same numerical value on both scales
Converting instrument readings to the absolute values needed by formulae

blocks.markdown: A **manometer** measures pressure differences using a column of liquid of density $\rho$ (kg/m$^3$). In a fluid at rest, pressure increases with depth by $\rho g h$, where $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$ and $h$ is the height of the column in m. So a height difference $h$ between the two liquid levels in a U-tube represents a pressure difference:

blocks.caption: Result in Pa when $\rho$ in kg/m$^3$, $g$ in m/s$^2$ and $h$ in m; divide by 1000 for kPa

blocks.title: Mercury manometer
blocks.prompt: A mercury (density 13 600 kg/m$^3$) U-tube manometer shows a level difference of 0.25 m. Find the pressure difference in kPa.
blocks.answer: The pressure difference is 33.4 kPa. The tube diameter does not matter.

blocks.title: Gas tank with an oil manometer
blocks.prompt: A U-tube manometer with oil (density 850 kg/m$^3$) is connected to a gas tank. The oil level in the open arm is 0.30 m higher than in the arm connected to the tank, and atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa. Find the absolute gas pressure.

steps.text: Gauge pressure from the column height.

blocks.answer: The gas is at about 103.8 kPa absolute.

blocks.markdown: How can a thermometer give a meaningful number at all? The answer is the **zeroth law of thermodynamics**: if body A is in thermal equilibrium with body C, and body B is also in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Taking C as a thermometer, equal readings on A and B mean they have the same temperature and no heat would pass between them if they were brought into contact.

blocks.title: Zeroth law and thermometers
blocks.text: A thermometer works because it comes into thermal equilibrium with the body being measured. The reading is the thermometer's own temperature, so you must wait until it settles and the thermometer must not disturb the body appreciably.

blocks.title: Unit slips
blocks.text: kPa and Pa differ by a factor of 1000. A pressure in bar is 100 kPa. Celsius must be converted to kelvin before ratios, not after.

points: Absolute pressure equals gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure, or atmospheric minus vacuum reading.
Absolute temperature in kelvin is Celsius plus 273.15; temperature differences are equal in K and C.
A manometer gives pressure difference rho g h, independent of tube diameter.
The zeroth law (equilibrium is transitive) is the basis of thermometers: bodies with the same reading are in thermal equilibrium.

questions.stem: A pressure gauge on a compressed-air receiver reads 600 kPa when the atmosphere is 100 kPa. What is the absolute pressure?

options.text: 500 kPa
600 kPa
700 kPa
6000 kPa

distractorRationale.d: Wrong by an order of magnitude.

questions.explanation: Gauge pressure is measured relative to the atmosphere, so p_abs = p_gauge + p_atm = 600 + 100 = 700 kPa. Absolute pressure is needed in equations of state.

questions.stem: Which statement is the zeroth law of thermodynamics?

options.text: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other
Energy is conserved
Heat flows from hot to cold
Entropy of an isolated system increases

questions.correctOptionText: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other

distractorRationale.c: This is a consequence of the second law.

questions.explanation: The zeroth law states that thermal equilibrium is transitive. It justifies using a thermometer as the third body C to compare temperatures.

questions.stem: Two U-tube manometers use the same liquid and show the same height difference, but one tube has twice the internal diameter. How do their pressure differences compare?

options.text: The wider tube shows twice the pressure difference
They are equal, because delta p = rho g h does not depend on diameter
The wider tube shows half the pressure difference
They cannot be compared

questions.correctOptionText: They are equal, because delta p = rho g h does not depend on diameter

distractorRationale.a: Cross-section does not affect hydrostatic pressure.
distractorRationale.c: Pressure does not scale with area.
distractorRationale.d: They can, since the formula only needs rho, g and h.

questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure difference depends only on the liquid density, gravitational acceleration and vertical height. Tube diameter does not appear in the formula.

questions.stem: A vacuum gauge on a condenser reads 30 kPa of vacuum when the atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa. What is the absolute pressure?

options.text: 130 kPa
70 kPa
30 kPa
-30 kPa

questions.explanation: A vacuum reading shows how far below atmosphere the pressure is. So p_abs = p_atm - p_vac = 100 - 30 = 70 kPa.

questions.stem: A thermometer reads 40 C when placed in liquid A, and also reads 40 C when placed in liquid B. What does the zeroth law allow you to conclude?

options.text: A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other, so no heat flows when they are brought into contact
A and B contain the same energy
A and B have the same mass
A and B must be the same substance

questions.correctOptionText: A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other, so no heat flows when they are brought into contact

distractorRationale.b: Equal temperature does not mean equal energy.

questions.explanation: Both liquids are in equilibrium with the thermometer, so by transitivity they are in equilibrium with each other. Equal temperature means no net heat flows between them, but says nothing about their masses or energy content.

questions.stem: A boiler pressure gauge reads 1.8 MPa when the barometer shows 98 kPa. Find the absolute pressure in kPa.
questions.explanation: The gauge reading in kPa is 1800, so p_abs = 1800 + 98 = 1898 kPa. Converting MPa to kPa first avoids unit slips.

questions.stem: A mercury (13 600 kg/m$^3$) manometer shows a level difference of 120 mm. Use g = 9.81 m/s$^2$. Find the pressure difference in kPa.
questions.explanation: The pressure difference is rho g h = 13600 x 9.81 x 0.12 = 16010 Pa = 16.01 kPa. The 120 mm must be converted to 0.12 m.

questions.stem: A U-tube manometer containing water (1000 kg/m$^3$) is connected to a sealed vessel of air. The water level in the open arm is 0.85 m above that in the arm connected to the vessel, and the atmospheric pressure is 99.5 kPa. Use g = 9.81 m/s$^2$. Find the absolute pressure of the air in kPa.
questions.explanation: The gauge pressure is 1000 x 9.81 x 0.85 = 8338 Pa = 8.338 kPa. Adding atmospheric pressure gives 107.84 kPa absolute.

questions.stem: Explain why absolute temperature and absolute pressure must be used in thermodynamic equations such as pV = mRT. Convert a gauge pressure of 150 kPa (atmosphere 101 kPa) and a temperature of 25 C to the values to use.
markingGuide: Equations are derived with zero pressure and zero temperature at physical zero
Gauge and Celsius have offsets, so using them gives wrong ratios
Temperature differences are the same in K and C
questions.explanation: Ratios such as T2/T1 and p2/p1 are only meaningful from a true zero. Converting gives 251 kPa and 298.15 K, which are the values to place in the equations of state.

questions.stem: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain how it makes temperature measurement with a thermometer meaningful.
markingGuide: If A and C are in thermal equilibrium and B and C are in thermal equilibrium, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium
Thermometer plays the role of body C
Equal readings on two bodies means same temperature, so no heat flows between them
Reading must be taken after the thermometer reaches equilibrium with the body
questions.explanation: The law justifies comparing bodies through a third one: the thermometer. A reading is valid only when equilibrium has been reached so that the thermometer shares the body's temperature.
